title: How Your Lungs Work
summary: How the lungs and diaphragm move air in and out, how oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it, and how to protect your lungs.
poll: Breathing is the most important job the body does.

versions.title: Your Lungs
versions.text:
Take a deep breath. Feel your chest get big. Now let it out. You just used your lungs!

You have two lungs. They are in your chest. Your ribs keep them safe.

Why do you breathe? Your body needs oxygen. Oxygen is in the air. Your lungs take it in. Then your blood takes it all through your body.

Your body makes a waste gas, too. Your lungs push it out. That is why you breathe out.

A big flat muscle sits below your lungs. It pulls down. Air rushes in. It goes back up. Air goes out.

Air comes in through your nose. Small hairs in your nose catch dust. Dust is bad for your lungs. Smoke is bad, too.

When you run, you breathe fast. Your body needs more oxygen.

In Saudi Arabia, there can be dust storms. Stay in on those days. Or wear a mask. Keep your lungs safe!

versions.title: How Your Lungs Work
versions.text:
Take a deep breath and hold it for a moment, and you will feel your chest grow bigger. Now breathe out slowly. In just a few seconds, your lungs have done an important job that they repeat all day and all night.

You have two lungs inside your chest. They are soft and spongy, and your ribs curve around them like a cage to keep them safe.

Every part of your body needs a gas called oxygen to stay alive. When you breathe in, air travels through your nose or mouth and down a tube called the windpipe. The windpipe splits into two smaller tubes, one for each lung. Inside the lungs, the oxygen moves into your blood, and then your heart pumps that blood all over your body.

Your body also makes a waste gas called carbon dioxide. Your blood carries it back to your lungs, and you get rid of it each time you breathe out.

Breathing depends on a muscle called the diaphragm, which sits under your lungs like a dome. When it tightens and pulls down, your chest gets bigger and air rushes in. When it relaxes and moves up, air is pushed out again.

Your nose helps protect your lungs. Tiny hairs and a sticky liquid called mucus trap dust before it can reach them, which matters because dust and smoke can harm your lungs.

When you are resting, you breathe slowly and gently. When you run or play, you breathe faster, because your busy muscles need more oxygen.

In Saudi Arabia, strong winds sometimes bring dust storms. On those days, it is wise to stay inside or to wear a mask that covers your nose and mouth.

versions.title: Inside Your Lungs
versions.text:
Take a deep breath and hold it for a moment, and you will feel your chest expand. When you breathe out slowly, your lungs have completed an essential task that they repeat roughly twenty thousand times every day, usually without you noticing at all.

You have two lungs inside your chest, and although they look like large balloons, they are actually soft and spongy. Your ribs curve around them to form a protective cage, and the left lung is slightly smaller than the right to leave room for your heart.

Every cell in your body requires oxygen to release energy from food, so when you inhale, air travels through your nose or mouth and down the windpipe, which divides into two tubes called bronchi, one leading to each lung, and these branch again and again into thinner tubes, ending in hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli. Each air sac is wrapped in capillaries, the smallest blood vessels, and oxygen passes through their thin walls into the blood. Your heart then pumps this oxygen-rich blood throughout your body.

Meanwhile, your cells produce a waste gas called carbon dioxide, which moves from the blood into the alveoli so that you can remove it when you exhale.

Breathing depends on a dome-shaped muscle called the diaphragm, located beneath your lungs. When it contracts and flattens, your chest becomes larger and air rushes in, and when it relaxes and rises, air is pushed back out.

Your nose protects your lungs, because tiny hairs and a sticky liquid called mucus trap dust before it can travel deeper inside. This matters, since dust and smoke can damage delicate lung tissue.

During exercise, you breathe faster and more deeply, because your hard-working muscles demand additional oxygen.

An adult at rest breathes roughly twelve to twenty times each minute, while children usually breathe a little faster. Regular exercise strengthens the diaphragm and the other muscles used for breathing, whereas smoking damages the delicate tissue of the lungs and makes every breath more difficult.

In Saudi Arabia, powerful winds occasionally create dust storms, so on those days it is sensible to remain indoors or wear a protective mask.

versions.title: Inside Your Lungs
versions.text:
Tucked safely within the protective cage formed by your ribs sit two soft, spongy lungs, with the left lung built slightly smaller than the right in order to make room for the heart nestled beside it. Every single cell throughout your body requires a continuous supply of oxygen in order to release usable energy from the food you eat, and your lungs exist precisely to capture that oxygen from the surrounding air and deliver it into your bloodstream.

When you inhale, air travels in through your nose or mouth and down your windpipe, which then splits into two separate bronchi, one directing air into each lung. From there, the bronchi branch repeatedly into progressively narrower passages, eventually terminating in hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli. Each individual alveolus is wrapped tightly in a dense network of capillaries, the smallest blood vessels found anywhere in the human body, and it is here, across the impossibly thin walls separating air sac from blood vessel, that oxygen diffuses directly into the bloodstream. Your heart then pumps this freshly oxygenated blood throughout the entire body, delivering vital oxygen to every tissue and organ.

Carbon dioxide, a waste gas produced as cells use up oxygen, travels in exactly the opposite direction, moving from the blood back into the alveoli, where it is ultimately removed from the body each time you exhale.

The entire process of breathing is powered by the diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle positioned directly below the lungs. When the diaphragm contracts and flattens, the chest cavity enlarges and air rushes in to fill the expanding space, producing an inhale; when the diaphragm instead relaxes and rises back into its resting position, air is pushed back out, producing an exhale.

Your nose offers additional protection for the delicate lungs beyond, using tiny hairs and sticky mucus to trap dust and other particles before they can travel further down into the respiratory system. At rest, a typical healthy adult breathes somewhere between twelve and twenty times per minute, while children generally breathe somewhat faster than adults do. During exercise, both the rate and depth of breathing increase substantially, since working muscles demand considerably more oxygen than muscles at rest, and regular exercise over time helps strengthen the diaphragm and other muscles involved in breathing.

Smoking, by contrast, damages the lungs' delicate internal tissue and reduces its natural elasticity, making every single breath noticeably harder to draw. During Saudi Arabia's occasional dust storms, it is wise to stay indoors or wear a protective mask, since breathing in dust-laden air can irritate the lungs. Remarkably, breathing continues entirely automatically even while you sleep, repeating roughly 20,000 times over the course of an average day without any conscious effort at all.

versions.title: Inside Your Lungs
versions.text:
Tucked securely within the protective bony cage formed by your ribs sit two soft, spongy lungs, with the left lung deliberately constructed slightly smaller than its right counterpart in order to accommodate the heart nestled immediately beside it. Every single cell distributed throughout your body requires a continuous and uninterrupted supply of oxygen in order to release usable energy from the food you consume, and your lungs exist for precisely this purpose: to capture oxygen from the surrounding atmospheric air and subsequently deliver it efficiently into your circulating bloodstream.

When you inhale, air travels inward through either your nose or mouth and descends down your windpipe, which subsequently divides into two separate bronchi, each directing incoming air into one of the two lungs. From this point, the bronchi branch repeatedly into progressively narrower passages, ultimately terminating in hundreds of millions of microscopic air sacs known as alveoli. Each individual alveolus is wrapped tightly in a dense surrounding network of capillaries, the smallest blood vessels found anywhere within the human body, and it is precisely here, across the impossibly thin membranous walls separating air sac from adjacent blood vessel, that oxygen diffuses directly and efficiently into the circulating bloodstream. Your heart subsequently pumps this freshly oxygenated blood continuously throughout the entire body, delivering vital, life-sustaining oxygen to every tissue and organ system.

Carbon dioxide, a waste gas generated as individual cells consume oxygen, travels in precisely the opposite direction, moving steadily from the bloodstream back into the alveoli, where it is ultimately expelled from the body each time you exhale.

The entire mechanical process of breathing is powered by the diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscular structure positioned directly beneath the lungs. When the diaphragm contracts and flattens, the surrounding chest cavity correspondingly enlarges and air rushes inward to fill the newly expanded space, producing what we experience as an inhale; conversely, when the diaphragm instead relaxes and rises back toward its original resting position, air is forcefully pushed back outward, producing what we experience as an exhale.

Your nose additionally provides supplementary protection for the delicate lungs located further within, employing tiny hairs and sticky mucus specifically to trap dust particles and other airborne contaminants before they can travel deeper into the respiratory system. While at rest, a typical healthy adult breathes somewhere between twelve and twenty times per minute, whereas children generally breathe somewhat more rapidly than adults do under comparable conditions. During vigorous exercise, both the rate and depth of breathing increase substantially, since actively working muscles demand considerably more oxygen than muscles remaining at rest, and consistent regular exercise over extended periods helps progressively strengthen the diaphragm and other muscles directly involved in breathing.

Smoking, by stark contrast, progressively damages the lungs' delicate internal tissue and measurably reduces its natural elasticity, making every single subsequent breath noticeably harder to draw successfully. During Saudi Arabia's occasional dust storms, it is consistently wise to remain indoors or wear a protective mask, since breathing in dust-laden air can significantly irritate the sensitive lungs. Remarkably, breathing continues entirely automatically even while you sleep soundly, repeating roughly 20,000 times over the course of an average day without requiring any conscious effort whatsoever.

MID.prompt: Describe the path that air takes when you breathe in, and explain what happens to the oxygen and the carbon dioxide.
checklist: I described the path of air in the correct order.
I explained what happens to oxygen and to carbon dioxide.
I used words such as windpipe, diaphragm, and carbon dioxide.
MID.modelAnswer: When I breathe in, air travels through my nose or mouth, down my windpipe, and into my two lungs, with the diaphragm muscle tightening and pulling down to make my chest bigger so air rushes in. Inside my lungs, oxygen moves from the air into my blood so it can be carried all over my body. At the same time, my blood brings back carbon dioxide, a waste gas, and I get rid of it every time I breathe out.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how the structure of the lungs, from the bronchi to the alveoli, helps the body get oxygen. Use details from the article.
checklist: I described the branching path from the windpipe to the alveoli.
I explained how oxygen and carbon dioxide move through the capillaries.
I used precise words such as inhale, exhale, bronchi, and alveoli.
HIGH.modelAnswer: When I inhale, air travels down my windpipe, which splits into bronchi that branch again and again inside each lung until they reach tiny air sacs called alveoli. At the alveoli, oxygen passes into the blood through thin-walled capillaries that wrap around them, and the blood then carries that oxygen throughout my body. At the same time, carbon dioxide moves from the capillaries back into the alveoli, and I release it when I exhale, showing how this branching structure is perfectly built for exchanging gases with my blood.
